title: Bodies of Three Keralites Killed in Germany Fire to Arrive in Kochi on October 20
excerpt: The remains of Anjali S. Joy, Nova Sabu and Sivin Johny will be flown out of Germany on Monday evening and received at Nedumbassery airport on Tuesday, with the Kerala government bearing the transport cost.
body:
• The bodies of Anjali S. Joy, Nova Sabu and Sivin Johny, killed in the October 13 apartment fire in Bochum, Germany, will reach Kerala on Tuesday, October 20.
  • The Indian Embassy arranged for the bodies to be handed to a funeral home without post-mortems, at the families' request; cargo booking is being finalised and the bodies will be flown out on Monday evening.
  • The Kerala government will bear the transport cost of about €3,000 (roughly ₹3,00,000) per body, and ambulances will take the remains from Nedumbassery airport to their homes in Kollam, Idukki and Ernakulam districts.
  • German investigators are treating the fire as an arson attack; preliminary findings point to personal enmity between the flat owner and a Romanian national who is in police custody.

The bodies of the three young Keralites killed in an apartment fire in the German city of Bochum will be brought back to Kerala on Tuesday, October 20, The Hindu reported. The announcement ends days of waiting for the families of Anjali S. Joy, 27, from Kollam, Nova Sabu, 25, from Idukki, and Sivin Johny from Ernakulam, whose return we have been following since our earlier coverage of the families' wait for repatriation.

"Joy, 27, from Kollam, Nova Sabu, 25, from Idukki, and Sivin Johny from Ernakulam, whose return we have been following since our earlier coverage of the families' wait for repatriation ."

How the Repatriation Was Arranged

Acting on the families' request, the Indian Embassy arranged for the bodies to be handed over to a local funeral home without conducting post-mortems. G. Devarajan, the Kerala government's special representative in Delhi, said cargo booking formalities were being finalised and the bodies would be flown out by Monday evening.

https://x.com/TheSouthfirst/status/2111341438139031679

The return slipped by a day because funeral homes were closed on Sunday. A further hurdle arose when cargo flights initially had space for only two bodies; authorities ensured all three would travel home together rather than separately. The state government will bear the transportation cost of approximately €3,000, roughly ₹3,00,000, per body. On arrival at Nedumbassery airport, the remains will be taken to their respective homes in ambulances arranged by the government.

The Three Victims

All three had moved to Germany within the last few months for study and work. Sivin Johny, from Kalady in Ernakulam district, had arrived last month and was expected to start a job this week; his brother Salvin is studying nursing in Germany. Anjali Sheela Joy, from Kollam, had moved in July and was working part-time while looking for a teaching position. Nova Sabu, from Kattappana in Idukki, had also relocated in July to study while working part-time as a gym trainer, according to Mirror Now. Kerala Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan had said the state, through NORKA Roots, would coordinate with the Ministry of External Affairs and the Indian Embassy in Germany and bear the repatriation expenses.

The Bochum Fire and the Investigation

The fire broke out in the early hours of October 13 in a residential building in Bochum. Five other residents were injured, several with severe smoke inhalation, as flames spread up the stairwell and complicated rescue efforts. German police arrested a 41-year-old Romanian national who lived in the building on suspicion of murder, and investigators ruled out a technical defect.

That investigation continues. Preliminary findings reported by The Hindu indicate the tragedy stemmed from personal enmity between the flat owner and the Romanian national now in police custody. The arrest does not establish guilt, and German authorities have not yet announced formal charges or a confirmed cause.

What Happens Next

For the three families, Tuesday's arrival at Nedumbassery is the point at which funeral arrangements at home can finally be made, a week after the fire. For readers with family studying or working in Germany, the case is also a reminder of the practical chain that follows a death abroad: embassy intervention, funeral-home release, cargo booking and state support through NORKA Roots were all required before a return date could be set. The German investigation into the suspected arson, and the condition of the injured residents, remain open.
